title: Rajnath Singh's Vietnam and South Korea Tour Is India's Clearest Indo-Pacific Signal Yet
excerpt: A potential $700-million BrahMos deal with Vietnam, submarine modernisation talks with Seoul, and a strategic message aimed squarely at Beijing — the defence minister's two-nation visit is about far more than ceremony
body:
When Defence Minister Rajnath Singh boards his flight to Hanoi on May 18, he carries more than a diplomatic brief. He carries a message — to Beijing, to Washington, and to India's own strategic establishment — that New Delhi's Indo-Pacific ambitions have moved from rhetoric to hardware.

The two-nation tour, covering Vietnam (May 18-19) and South Korea (May 19-21), comes at a moment of heightened geopolitical tension in Asia. China's military assertiveness in the South China Sea, its deepening defence ties with Russia, and its economic leverage over ASEAN states have created an opening for India to position itself as an alternative security partner. Singh's visit is designed to exploit that opening.

## Vietnam: The BrahMos Question

The centrepiece of the Vietnam leg is the potential sale of BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles — a deal reportedly worth $700 million that has been under negotiation for over two years. If finalised, it would be India's largest-ever defence export and would make Vietnam only the second country, after the Philippines, to operate the BrahMos system.

The strategic logic is clear. Vietnam, which shares a contested maritime border with China in the South China Sea, has been seeking to modernise its deterrence capabilities. BrahMos, jointly developed by India and Russia, offers a shore-based anti-ship capability that would significantly complicate Chinese naval calculations in the region.

Beyond BrahMos, Singh is expected to sign a joint vision statement marking the tenth anniversary of India and Vietnam's Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, upgraded last year to an Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership. The visit will also include discussions on maritime domain awareness, joint naval exercises, and defence technology transfer.

## South Korea: Submarines and Semiconductors

The Seoul leg of the tour is less dramatic but potentially more consequential for India's long-term defence-industrial base. Discussions are expected to cover South Korea's expertise in submarine construction — relevant as India seeks to expand its conventional submarine fleet under Project 76 — and in defence electronics, where Korean firms have a technological edge.

South Korea's own Indo-Pacific Strategy, announced in 2023, aligns with India's Act East Policy in ways that previous Korean governments had resisted. The current administration in Seoul has been more willing to frame its security posture in terms that implicitly acknowledge the China challenge, creating common ground with New Delhi.

Defence sources indicate that Singh will also explore Korean investment in India's defence corridors in Uttar Pradesh and Tamil Nadu, where the government is trying to build manufacturing ecosystems that can support both domestic needs and export contracts.

## The China Subtext

Neither India nor its partners will name China explicitly in joint statements. They never do. But the subtext is unmistakable. India's deepening defence ties with Vietnam and South Korea — both nations with complex relationships with Beijing — represent a systematic effort to build a network of security partnerships that constrains Chinese influence without triggering open confrontation.

For India, which fought a deadly border clash with China in 2020 and continues to face tensions along the Line of Actual Control, the Indo-Pacific strategy is not abstract. It is an extension of a neighbourhood security challenge. By selling defence hardware to Vietnam and buying defence technology from South Korea, India creates interdependencies that make its strategic partnerships harder to unwind.

## The Diaspora Dimension

India's defence exports have become a point of pride for the diaspora, particularly in the United States, where the BrahMos deal has been covered as evidence of India's emergence as a net security provider rather than merely a buyer. For Indian-Americans working in defence and technology, the growing India-South Korea technology partnership opens potential professional bridges.

Singh's visit coincides with the 136th birth anniversary of Ho Chi Minh, a historical figure whose connections with India — he visited Kolkata and was influenced by Indian independence movements — add a layer of diplomatic sentiment to the proceedings. Whether sentiment translates into signed contracts will determine if this is a milestone visit or merely a ceremonial one.
